questions.question_text:
Two similar shapes have matching sides in the ratio $2:3$.
What is the ratio of their areas?

options.why: Left the ratio as the length ratio; areas scale by the square, not unchanged.
Cubed each term (the volume rule) instead of squaring for area.
Squared only the second term instead of both terms.

questions.question_text:
Two similar solids have matching edges in the ratio $3:4$.
What is the ratio of their volumes?

options.why: Left the ratio as the edge ratio; volumes scale by the cube.
Squared each term (the area rule) instead of cubing for volume.
Cubed only the second term instead of both terms.

questions.question_text:
The areas of two similar figures are in the ratio $16:81$.
What is the ratio of their matching sides?

options.why: Forgot to take the square root of the area ratio.
Took the square root of only the first term.
Squared the ratio instead of taking the square root.

questions.question_text:
The volumes of two similar solids are in the ratio $8:27$.
What is the ratio of their matching edges?

options.why: Forgot to take the cube root of the volume ratio.
Took the cube root of only the first term.
Took the cube root of only the second term.

questions.question_text:
A shape is enlarged by scale factor $5$.
Its original area is $8\text{ cm}^2$.
What is the area of the enlarged shape?

options.why: Multiplied the area by the scale factor instead of its square.
Cubed the scale factor (volume rule) instead of squaring.
Gave the area factor $5^2=25$ but forgot to multiply the original area.

questions.question_text:
A solid is enlarged by scale factor $2$.
Its original volume is $15\text{ cm}^3$.
What is the volume of the enlarged solid?

options.why: Multiplied the volume by the scale factor instead of its cube.
Squared the scale factor (area rule) instead of cubing.
Gave the volume factor $2^3=8$ but forgot to multiply the original volume.
Multiplied by the length ratio $3$ instead of the area ratio $3^2$.
Cubed the length ratio (volume rule) instead of squaring.
Squared the given area instead of applying the area ratio.
Multiplied by the length ratio $2$ instead of the volume ratio $2^3$.
Squared the length ratio (area rule) instead of cubing.
Squared the given volume instead of applying the volume ratio.

questions.question_text:
Two similar solids have matching lengths in the ratio $2:3$.
What are the ratio of their areas and the ratio of their volumes?
$\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{Lengths} & \text{Areas} & \text{Volumes} \\ \hline 2:3 & ? & ? \end{array}$

options.why: Applied no power to either ratio.
Swapped the rules: cubed for area and squared for volume.
Squared for both, forgetting volume needs the cube.

questions.question_text:
Two similar cylinders have surface areas in the ratio $9:25$.
What is the ratio of their volumes?

options.why: Used the surface-area ratio as the volume ratio.
Gave the length ratio instead of continuing to the volume ratio.
Squared the area ratio instead of going via the length ratio.

questions.question_text:
A large candle is melted down and recast into smaller similar candles, each with $\frac{1}{3}$ of the height of the original.
How many smaller candles can be made?

options.why: Used the length ratio $3$ instead of cubing it for volume.
Squared the ratio (area rule) instead of cubing.
Raised the ratio to the fourth power instead of the third.

questions.solution_text:
Each small candle has volume $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^3=\frac{1}{27}$ of the original.
Number of candles $=1\div\frac{1}{27}$
$=27$

questions.question_text:
A map is drawn to a scale of $1:500$.
A field has an actual area of $250\,000\text{ cm}^2$.
What is its area on the map?

options.why: Divided by the scale $500$ instead of its square $500^2$.
Divided by $2\times500$ instead of $500^2$.
Gave the actual area, forgetting to scale it down to the map.
